title: Backward Kolmogorov equation
description: The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process $dX_t = -X_t\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t$ ($\Psi = \frac{x^2 + y^2}{2}$, σ = 1) with all 2000 particles started at one point, $x = (2, 0)$. The particle mean of $f(X_t)$ is then a Monte Carlo estimate of $v(x, t) = \mathbb{E}[f(X_t) \mid X_0 = x]$, the solution of the backward Kolmogorov equation $\partial_t v = -\nabla\Psi\cdot\nabla v + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\Delta v$ with $v(x, 0) = f(x)$ (course notes, §4.4.2 and §5.2.3). Here $f(x) = x_1^2$, and exactly $v(x, t) = x_1^2 e^{-2t} + \frac{\sigma^2}{2}(1 - e^{-2t})$. Press play and step with → to stop at a given time.

questions.text: Pause at $t = 1$. Particle mean of $(X^1_t)^2$, i.e. $v((2, 0), 1)$?
What does $v(x, t)$ converge to as $t \to \infty$, whatever the starting point?
The dashed line is $\int f\,d\pi$ under the stationary (Gibbs) law. How is it related to the limit of $v(x, t)$?
Check that the exact $v(x, t)$ above solves $\partial_t v = -x_1\,\partial_{x_1} v + \frac12\,\partial_{x_1 x_1} v$.
To get $v$ at every $x$ with this method you need one run per starting point. When is that still better than solving the PDE on a grid? (Think of dimension and of needing only a few points.)
Duality: the forward (Fokker–Planck) and backward equations give the same $\mathbb{E} f(X_t)$. Which object does each one evolve: the density or the test function?
